**Approaches message — after the recorded answers**

I recommend **reusing the existing CSV serializer and adding paging**, as you selected. The button will sit beside the report title, and exports will use the visible table columns in table order.

Paging is explicitly unimplemented according to the gather draft. Primary-code lookups of the report loader, its paging contract, serializer callers, and performance-test setup are unavailable in this exercise; their compatibility remains unverified. In particular, the supplied observations establish neither a timing baseline nor that either approach meets the ticket’s under-60-second requirement.

The distinguishing axis is **when rows are serialized and how much report data is retained in memory**.

### 1. Fetch all pages, then serialize — recommended reuse-first approach

Extend the existing report-loading path with paging, collect the complete report, and pass it through the existing CSV serializer using the visible columns in table order.

This keeps serialization on the established path and avoids introducing a separate export service or parallel column schema. Its main trade-off is retaining the complete report in memory before serialization. Changes to a shared loader could also affect its other callers; that blast radius must be established before implementation.

Removes: none.
Adds: the title-adjacent Export CSV button and handler; paging behavior on the existing report-loading path; export orchestration; button, column-order, complete-report, failure, and 10k-row timing tests.
Pattern: follows the table-column reuse reported for `src/export/csv.ts`; extends existing responsibilities rather than duplicating the serializer.

### 2. Fetch pages and serialize incrementally

Keep the same button, column selection, serializer ownership, and paging requirement, but extend the serializer to consume pages incrementally rather than requiring the complete report up front.

This drops the gather draft’s implicit assumption that reusing the serializer means supplying one fully materialized table-shaped dataset. It could reduce retained row data, but incremental serialization introduces additional concerns: writing the header once, preserving row order across pages, and handling a failure after some CSV content has been produced. Whether it improves total completion time remains unverified.

Removes: none.
Adds: the title-adjacent Export CSV button and handler; paging behavior on the existing report-loading path; incremental-input behavior in `src/export/csv.ts`; export orchestration; button, column-order, page-boundary, failure, and 10k-row timing tests.
Pattern: preserves the column-definition ownership reported for `src/export/csv.ts`, but changes its input contract and therefore requires regression coverage for retained callers.

An independent serializer or separately maintained export-column schema is not a viable candidate under your recorded choice to reuse the serializer and export the visible columns in order.

I would switch the recommendation to incremental serialization if code inspection or representative 10k-row measurements show that full-report collection cannot meet the timing requirement or creates unacceptable memory pressure.
